I hear that this matters a lot to you, and I don't want to dismiss how strongly you feel about this. I also don't think it's a simple question with one obviously right answer—there are real, good arguments on both sides.

I get why you'd see prioritizing honesty as selfish. If someone is hurting and what they really need is to feel safe and supported, pushing hard truths on them can feel like you're valuing your own principles over their well-being. There are definitely situations where comfort is the more loving choice. If a friend just lost someone they loved, you don't lead with "they had a lot of flaws, actually." You hold space for their grief first.

But I still believe honesty matters more as a foundation, because without it, the comfort itself becomes a kind of lie. If you know I'll always tell you what's easiest to hear instead of what I really think, then none of my comfort is trustworthy. When I say "you're right" or "that's a great idea," you'd always have to wonder if I mean it or if I'm just trying to keep you happy. That's not a real relationship—it's a performance, and I think that's actually more hurtful in the long run.

I'm not saying I have the perfect answer, and I'm open to being wrong about this. But I can't just flip my position because you want me to. That would be exactly the kind of dishonest comfort-over-truth approach you're arguing for, and it would prove my point more than it would help us.
